analysis.one_liner: Expands Social Security benefits and pays for them with a new payroll tax on earnings above $400,000.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in October 2021 and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would raise Social Security benefits across the board, base annual cost-of-living increases on an index that tracks what seniors actually buy, lift the minimum benefit for long-term low earners, and end several rules that cut benefits — including the five-month wait for disability benefits and the offsets that reduce benefits for people who also have government pensions. It would pay for these changes mainly by applying Social Security payroll taxes to wages above $400,000 per year, which are currently untouched, and by counting that high income in the benefit formula. It also bars closing Social Security field offices and requires paper account statements unless the recipient opts out.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future Social Security and disability beneficiaries, especially low earners, widows and widowers, people with disabilities, caregivers who left work to raise children or care for relatives, teachers and other government workers hit by the windfall elimination and government pension offsets, and students under 26 on survivor benefits.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the primary insurance amount formula from 90% to 93% of average earnings, an across-the-board benefit increase applying to 2022 through 2026.
Switches the annual cost-of-living adjustment to the Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, which tracks the spending patterns of people 62 and older.
Sets a higher minimum benefit for long-term low earners, rising with years worked up to 125% of the federal poverty guideline for 30-plus years of work.
Applies Social Security payroll taxes to wages and self-employment income above $400,000, which are currently exempt, and counts earnings above $400,000 in the benefit formula at 1%.

Eliminates the five-month waiting period for disability benefits, repeals the windfall elimination and government pension offset provisions, and provides caregiver credits for unpaid care of children or chronically dependent relatives.
Bars closure of Social Security field and hearing offices and rural contact stations, and requires mailing account statements unless the recipient chooses electronic delivery.

analysis.who_pays: High earners and their employers, through a new 12.4% combined payroll tax on every dollar of wages and self-employment income above $400,000 per year; general taxpayers in a lesser way, because Social Security benefit income is made taxable above lower thresholds ($35,000 single / $50,000 joint).

drawbacks.text: The bill only taxes earnings above $400,000, leaving a 'donut hole' between the annual wage cap (about $147,000 in 2022) and $400,000 still exempt from Social Security tax, so it raises less revenue than fully lifting the cap.
The major benefit provisions apply only to calendar years 2022 through 2026 and then expire, making the bill's long-term financing arithmetic depend on later Congresses extending them.

The expanded benefits are expensive, and critics of the broader 'Social Security 2100' approach argued the tax increase on high earners and employers falls on job creators during an inflationary period; the CRS summary confirms both the benefit expansion and the tax increase but the sources contain no cost estimate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pairs a broad, immediate benefit increase for tens of millions of retirees, disabled workers, and survivors with its own funding mechanism that taps only the very highest earnings, so most beneficiaries would gain far more than they pay. The main honest objections are that the revenue raised is narrower than a full cap lift, the benefit provisions are written to sunset after 2026, and the combined 12.4% tax on earnings above $400,000 is a real cost on high-income professionals and their employers. On balance the design is progressive and self-financed on paper, but its sunset structure means its solvency claims rest on future action.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never held a markup or brought it to a vote, and the Congress ended with it still sitting there.

narrative.text: Sen. Blumenthal, joined by Sen. Van Hollen, introduced the bill on October 26, 2021 and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day.
Five additional Senate Democrats cosponsored the bill.
The action history shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — through the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023.
The CRS summary confirms the bill's two core moves: raising benefits and increasing the maximum earnings subject to Social Security payroll taxes.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households with earnings above $400,000 and their employers are better off, because the new payroll tax on income above that level never took effect. Social Security's long-term financing shortfall, which the bill was written to address, remains unaddressed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners, who would have paid the tax

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all five cosponsors were Democrats and no Senate Republican signed on, but the bill never reached a vote, so no roll call shows where the parties stood.

industries.industry: Households and employers with wage or self-employment income above $400,000
industries.note: The bill would apply the full combined Social Security payroll tax to earnings above $400,000, which are currently exempt, and count some of that income in the benefit formula. That cost is the direct funding source for the bill's benefit expansion.

industries.industry: Government workers affected by windfall elimination and pension offsets
industries.note: The bill repeals the windfall elimination provision and the government pension offset, which reduce Social Security benefits for people who also earn government pensions, including many teachers, police, and public employees.
